questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)=x$

II. $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0$

III. $P(x,y)=y+{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=\frac{y}{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0\ne 1.
$$

- Pair II gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair III does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)={e}^{y}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x}$

II. $P(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=y$

III. $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=y$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{y}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}-{e}^{y}\ne 1.
$$

- Pair II does *not* give the required area.  Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{1}{1+{y}^{2}}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{1+{y}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

- Pair III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)=-\frac{y}{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\frac{x}{3}$

II. $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x$

III. $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{1}{3},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{2}{3}\ne 1.
$$

- Pair II gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair III does *not* give the required area. Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x-2y\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y}-y,\,x{e}^{y}⟩$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y},\,0⟩$

III. $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{5}+{x}^{7},\,\frac{6x}{5}⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I give the required area. In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{y}-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{e}^{y}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{y}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field III does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{5}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{6}{5},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{7}{5}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14243481/assets/c5eb703c2812d82848bb5a1639c2840c4abf9318b988087e2216d9881137da72.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{4}\,i+{t}^{3}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=\,i-t\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{8}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
